summary: Updates the wildcard definition from RFC 1034. It changes how wildcards interact with CNAME, removes an error condition and rewrites the wording for some central concepts. The goal is to refine the definition, not to change how wildcards behave. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A DNS wildcard answers for any name nobody wrote down specially. This memo cleans up the confusing rules about when the wildcard applies.

questions: what is a closest encloser in dns
how do wildcards work with cname records
subtitle: Clears up when a DNS wildcard answers a query, and fixes how wildcards and CNAME records interact.

tldr.problem: The wildcard definition in RFC 1034 was incomplete and confusing, and implementations diverged from it in different ways, which also tangled the design of DNSSEC authenticated denial.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new terms (wildcard domain name, asterisk label, closest encloser, source of synthesis), restates what it means for a name to exist, and adds a CNAME rule so a wildcard CNAME is handled like an exact-match CNAME.
tldr.outcome: Wildcard behavior is described precisely enough for interoperability, with only the CNAME change affecting implementations. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 2672.

today: RFC 4592 is a Proposed Standard from July 2006. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 2672, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Wildcards Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
Sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 of RFC 1034 describe how a name server synthesizes answers from special resource records called wildcards. That description was incomplete and confusing, and many implementations diverged from it. The push to fix it came from the DNS security extensions (RFC 4033): with an unclear wildcard definition, the design of authenticated denial became entangled.

The document aims to limit its changes. It does three things: defines new terms, makes minor changes to avoid conflicting concepts, and describes how certain record types act as wildcards. It stays inside the spirit of the original and avoids restricting implementation choices. It does not use RFC 2119 requirement words.

Only one change affects implementations: the CNAME rule. The new definition of existence is not a protocol impact, and the relaxed rule on asterisk labels is unlikely to matter because RFC 1034 never said when to enforce it.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook for wildcards had gaps, so different programs played by different rules. This new rulebook fills the gaps without changing the game.

sections.title: Wildcard Syntax
sections.content:
A wildcard is an ordinary resource record. The only special thing is its owner name. A wildcard domain name is a name whose leftmost label is an asterisk label: the two octets 0x01 0x2a, which is a one-octet label length followed by the ASCII code for the asterisk character. In RFC 1034's terms, a wildcard is a resource record owned by a wildcard domain name.

Labels such as the* and two asterisks in a row are not asterisk labels, so names starting with them are never wildcard domain names. Because wildcards are plain records, they are carried in zone transfers and incremental zone transfers like any other record.

RFC 1034 said the part after the leading asterisk label should not contain another asterisk label. That restriction is removed: it did not serve a purpose, and nested wildcard names are unambiguous once the closest encloser is defined. A wildcard domain name can have subdomains and can be an empty non-terminal.

A wildcard domain name is not special in a query's question section, where it only matches an identical asterisk label in the zone, or in record data, where an asterisk is just an asterisk.
sections.plainLanguage: A wildcard is a record whose name starts with a star, like a card that says "anyone not on the list". A star anywhere else is just a star.

sections.title: What It Means for a Name to Exist
sections.content:
A wildcard does not apply when the query name, or a name between the wildcard and the query name, exists. So existence matters, and RFC 1034 was unclear about it. A literal reading could imply that every possible name exists with no data, which contradicts the name error response RFC 1034 defines.

The new wording: nodes in the tree either own at least one RRSet or have descendants that collectively own one. A node with no RRSets may exist only if it has descendants that do; this is an empty non-terminal. Empty leaf nodes do not exist. A zone boundary name owns data such as the NS RRSet, so it exists.

The RFC's example zone for example. has *.example. with TXT and MX records, sub.*.example., host1.example., SRV records under _ssh._tcp and a delegation at subdel.example.. A query for host3.example. MX is answered from the wildcard. A query for host1.example. MX is not, because that name exists. A query for host3.example. A gets no error but no data, since the wildcard has no A RRSet. A query for foo.bar.example. TXT is answered from the wildcard because bar.example. does not exist.

A wildcard also "blocks itself": *.example. does not match names below *.example.. Covering those would need *.*.example..
sections.plainLanguage: A name counts as "on the list" if it has something written down, or if something below it does. The wildcard only helps names that are not on the list.

sections.title: How a Server Uses a Wildcard
sections.content:
The relevant algorithm is step 3, part 'c' of RFC 1034 section 4.3.2. The RFC stresses that the steps are not pseudo-code and need not run in order, as long as the result complies. Step 2 picks the nearest-ancestor zone, so all of step 3 happens inside one zone. Step 3 walks the query name label by label. It ends in exactly one of three ways: an exact match (part 'a'), a referral below a cut point (part 'b'), or no matching label (part 'c'). Matching ignores the query type.

In part 'c' the lookup has "fallen off the tree". The closest encloser is the existing node with the most labels matching the query name, counted from the root. It might be an empty non-terminal or even a wildcard domain name, but it is never used to synthesize records. The source of synthesis is the name *.<closest encloser>, provided it exists. If it does not exist there is no wildcard synthesis and no search for an alternative, so at most one place can supply synthetic records for a lookup.

If the source exists, its records matching the query type are copied into the answer with the owner set to the query name. The RFC's table shows host3.example. has closest encloser example. and source *.example., while foobar.*.example. has closest encloser *.example. and no source.

The one behavior change is for CNAME: if the data at the source of synthesis is a CNAME and the query type is not CNAME, the CNAME is copied into the answer with the owner changed to the query name, the query name becomes the CNAME target, and processing goes back to step 1. This mirrors the existing rule for an exact match.
sections.plainLanguage: The server walks down the name until it cannot go further, then looks for a star card right at that spot. If there is one, it answers using that card. If not, it gives up and does not look elsewhere.

sections.title: Wildcards of Special Record Types
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC walks through record types that have proven hard to understand when owned by a wildcard domain name.

  • SOA: the name would be a zone apex, which can never be a source of synthesis, but there is no reason to forbid it.
  • NS: left undefined, because synthesizing a delegation conflicts with DNSSEC's authorization model. Wildcard NS RRSets are discouraged operationally, but not barred.
  • CNAME: handled by the changed step 3c text above.
  • DNAME: a threat to the coherency of the DNS and to be avoided or outright rejected, because different caches would be fed different synthesized rules.
  • SRV: only the owner name matters, not the "Name" part of the SRV format, so _foo._udp.*.example. is not a wildcard owner.
  • DS: meaningless and harmless.
  • NSEC and RRSIG: present at wildcards in signed zones. Synthesized NSEC records only occur on an exact match and are not harmful, and the label count in an RRSIG tells verifiers to ignore the synthesized owner name.
  • Empty non-terminal wildcard: the response is no error with no RRSet in the answer section.
sections.plainLanguage: Some kinds of records behave oddly when they sit on a star card. The memo says which are fine, which to avoid, and which it leaves for another day.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it refines the specifications to make it more likely that security can be added to DNS. No functional additions are made. The aim is to keep DNS, its security and its extensions more predictable.

The DNSSEC link is why the document exists at all, and it shows up in the NS, NSEC and RRSIG discussions above.
sections.plainLanguage: Clear rules make it easier to add safety checks later, because everyone agrees what the answers should look like.
